raw_case_text:
A 72-year-old male hospitalized at an outside facility 2 months ago with lower-left lobe pneumonia treated with moxifloxacin for 12 days, and continuing symptoms of malaise, loss of appetite and weight loss, was referred to the emergency department with a symptomatic 4.9 cm AAA on CT scanning causing severe continuous lower abdominal and back pain requiring opiates and recurrent fever, up to 38.5 C. The latter symptom had started 12 days ago, although it had subsided 3 days later after receiving ciprofloxacin. Past medical history included COPD, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, and hyperuricemia. He was on formoterol and tiotropium inhalers, valsartan/hydrochlorothiazide, barnidipine, moxonidine, ezetimibe/simvastatin, sitagliptin/metformin, and allopurinol. He was an ex-smoker, while his occupation was sheep and goat keeper and slaughterer and he reported to consume raw dairy products, including home-made cheese made from unpasteurized milk. On presentation, he was hemodynamically stable, afebrile, while a tender AAA was noted. Leukocytosis (WBC 16,650/mm3 with a left shift) and raised CRP (29 mg/ dL, reference value <0.8 mg/dL) were found. Blood cultures were negative. He underwent an abdominal CTA with contrast ([Figures 1a-c and 2a-b]) with a 16 x MDCT scanner (Lightspeed 16, GE, Milwaukee, WI, USA). The nonenhanced scan revealed an infrarenal AAA with a maximum diameter of 4.9 cm, in the axial plane, aortic wall calcifications, some of them apparently discontinuous, and subtle periaortic fat stranding. The contrast-enhanced CT scan underwent multiplanar reformat using the maximum intensity projection (MIP) algorithm. The aortic wall was markedly irregular, with the presence of multiple contrast-filled saccular outpouchings. There was also evidence of periaortic soft-tissue attenuation mass and/or luminal thrombus. The abnormalities extended distally up to the level of the aortic bifurcation, and the proximal part of the right common iliac arteries. There was no evidence of contrast extravasation or hematoma in the retroperitoneal space. There was no evidence of gas in the region. The abdominal CT scan was otherwise unremarkable.
Based on the clinical picture, the history of an infectious disease (pneumonia) and CT findings, an infected AAA was suspected. Our patient was started meropenem 1gr TID and vancomycin 1gr BID and underwent urgent AAA repair with typical aortobifemoral bypass grafting using a 16 x 8 mm bifurcated e-PTFE graft (Advanta SST, Atrium Medical Corp, Hudson, NH, USA). Operative findings included an infrarenal AAA extending to the aortic bifurcation. The right common iliac artery was pulseless. The left common iliac artery had a whitish color. The intestine was adhered densely on the aneurysm. A small amount of dirty fluid inside the luminal thrombus was sent for culture along with aneurysmal wall samples and thrombus material for common bacteria, mycobacterium, and Brucella pathogens. Periaortic tissue and aortic wall were sent for histological examination. A part of the presumably infected aneurysmal sac was excised. The culture of the dirty fluid was positive for Listeria monocytogenes, sensitive to ampicillin, penicillin, vancomycin, teicoplanin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, and ofloxacin. Additionally, a multisensitive Staphylococcus epidermidis was isolated. Histology showed acute sac inflammation. Postoperative course was uneventful and on postoperative day 10, our patient was transferred to his regional hospital to complete a further 4-week course of intravenous antibiotics (meropenem 2gr TID and vancomycin 1gr BID) and an additional 4-week course of oral antibiotics (trimethoprime/sulfomethoxazole 800/160 mg BID) as an outpatient. Eleven months later our patient remains asymptomatic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old male sheep and goat keeper presented with a 12-day history of severe continuous lower abdominal and back pain and recurrent fever up to 38.5 C on a 2-month background of malaise, anorexia, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 72-year-old man who had been hospitalized 2 months earlier for left lower lobe pneumonia (treated with 12 days of moxifloxacin) experienced persistent malaise, anorexia, and weight loss, and developed severe opiate-requiring lower abdominal and back pain with recurrent fevers up to 38.5 C 12 days prior to emergency department referral (temporarily subsiding after 3 days of ciprofloxacin).
subjective.past_medical_history: COPD, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, and hyperuricemia; left lower lobe pneumonia 2 months prior. Former smoker; worked as a sheep and goat keeper and slaughterer and regularly consumed unpasteurized homemade cheese and raw dairy products. Home medications: formoterol and tiotropium inhalers, valsartan/hydrochlorothiazide, barnidipine, moxonidine, ezetimibe/simvastatin, sitagliptin/metformin, and allopurinol.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe lower abdominal and back pain, recurrent fever (38.5 C), malaise, anorexia, and weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Hemodynamically stable and afebrile on arrival (following pre-admission ciprofloxacin); palpable, tender infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 16,650/mm3 with a left shift, CRP 29 mg/dL (normal <0.8 mg/dL); peripheral blood cultures were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced 16-slice abdominal MDCT angiography demonstrated a 4.9 cm infrarenal AAA extending to the aortic bifurcation and proximal right common iliac artery with discontinuous mural calcifications, periaortic fat stranding, periaortic soft-tissue mass/luminal thrombus, and multiple contrast-filled saccular outpouchings without retroperitoneal rupture. Intraoperative exploration showed dense intestinal adhesions, a pulseless right common iliac artery, a whitish left common iliac artery, and turbid intrathrombus fluid; histopathology of the excised aneurysm wall confirmed acute sac inflammation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Aneurysmal wall and thrombus cultures for Brucella and mycobacteria were negative, whereas culture of the intraluminal aneurysm fluid grew Listeria monocytogenes (susceptible to ampicillin, penicillin, vancomycin, teicoplanin, erythromycin, chloramphenicol, and ofloxacin) and multisensitive Staphylococcus epidermidis, confirming a mycotic infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm caused by Listeria monocytogenes. Treated with urgent open aneurysm resection and aortobifemoral bypass grafting (16 x 8 mm bifurcated e-PTFE graft) plus 5.5 weeks of IV meropenem (1-2 g TID) and vancomycin (1 g BID) followed by 4 weeks of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (800/160 mg BID), remaining asymptomatic at 11-month follow-up.
